title: A Locker for the Homecoming
premise: Bram Lockridge has spent three years at Hollow Creek High perfecting the art of being invisible—no pronoun debates, no club sign-ups, no history. But when the school's legendary ghost, said to be a student who vanished in 1974, starts leaving notes in Bram's own handwriting and a name Bram has never told anyone, invisibility stops being an option. Following the notes leads Bram and two reluctant allies—archivist-in-training Priya and ghost-tour cynic Dez—into the sealed sub-basement beneath the gym, where the 'ghost' turns out to be a decades-old record of every student the school tried to erase, kept alive by a tradition of secret caretakers. In the end, Bram chooses to sign their real name to the archive, the school formally acknowledges the students it buried, and Bram graduates not as a label or a rumor but as the person who made remembering an act of belonging.
about_author: K. M. Voss is the pen name of a former substitute teacher who spent years listening to teenagers explain which hallways felt wrong. They write small-town gothic stories about the kids history files forget, and this is their second novel.

chapters.title: The Rules of Being New, Year Three
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Opening day at Hollow Creek High, where Bram rehearses the careful choreography of invisibility: no clubs, no questions, no real name on anything. The emotional beat is the ache of safety that costs everything, ending with Bram noticing the old locker 214 that no one is ever assigned.

chapters.title: Ink That Wasn't There Yesterday
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Inside locker 214, Bram finds a note addressed with a name Bram has only ever said aloud once, in a whisper, years ago. The ink shimmers wrong under the fluorescent lights. The beat is fear mixed with a terrifying thrill of being known.

chapters.title: Priya and the Card Catalog of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The school's unofficial historian, Priya keeps a binder of Hollow Creek legends and has been waiting for locker 214 to open. She corners Bram with evidence: the ghost wrote to a student in 1989, too. The beat is wary alliance—two careful kids recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Dez Doesn't Believe in Anything Free
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Ghost-tour cynic and custodian's kid, Dez knows the building's real secrets and thinks the notes are a cruel prank targeting Bram. When a second note appears mid-class in front of thirty witnesses, cynicism cracks. The beat is defensive loyalty turning to reluctant investment.

chapters.title: The Vanishing of Wren Alcott, 1974
chapters.summary: Priya's POV in the archives. The trio finds Wren Alcott's yearbook photo with the caption cut out and a disciplinary file that ends mid-sentence. Wren was, by every account, 'a student the school preferred not to discuss.' The beat is the chill of institutional erasure mirroring Bram's own self-erasure.

chapters.title: Notes in My Handwriting
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The third note is written in Bram's exact hand, saying something Bram has never written down. Dez suspects Bram is doing this for attention; Bram can't prove otherwise, even to themselves. The beat is the horror of doubting your own memory and identity.

chapters.title: Homecoming Committee, Population Three
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. As a cover—and because Priya insists the ghost only writes near the old gym—the trio joins homecoming planning, the one club Bram swore off. Bram gets assigned the 'heritage display.' The beat is belonging arriving sideways, disguised as a chore.

chapters.title: What the Custodian Keys Open
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Dez lifts the sub-basement key from their father's ring and leads the others past the boiler room to a door painted over so many times it's become part of the wall. Behind it: cold air, and the smell of old paper. The beat is the threshold crossing—no way back to careful.

chapters.title: The Room of Unassigned Names
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The sub-basement holds a card catalog and wall of folders: every student the school quietly pushed out since 1950, each with a note in the ghost's impossible ink. Wren Alcott's folder is the thickest—and the last page is blank, waiting. The beat is awe curdling into grief.

chapters.title: The Tradition of the Caretakers
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A hidden letter reveals the 'ghost' is a relay: each generation of targeted students became caretakers of the archive, and the ink is a chemical tradition, not a haunting. Wren didn't vanish—Wren was made the first keeper and stayed hidden until graduation. The beat is revelation that rewrites fear into inheritance.

chapters.title: Someone Else Is Reading the Files
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Folders have been moved, and a page about a current student—Bram—has gone missing. Someone in the present is curating the archive, and not kindly. The beat is the shift from mystery to threat: the past isn't the danger; the present is.

chapters.title: Vice Principal Hargrove's Neat Little School
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The trail leads to Hargrove, whose own name is in the catalog as a 1990s 'problem'—and who chose to become the school's fiercest enforcer of normal instead of its keeper. He's been removing folders to protect his reinvented self. The beat is a chilling mirror: what Bram could become if shame wins.

chapters.title: The Note That Used My Deadname
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Hargrove, exposed, retaliates by pinning a cruel note to Bram's locker using the name Bram buried—framing it as the ghost's work. The hallway watches. The beat is the lowest point: the labels going back on in front of everyone.

chapters.title: Priya Quits the Committee
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Humiliated by association and terrified her own catalog secrets will surface, Priya withdraws and nearly hands her binder to Hargrove as a peace offering. The beat is betrayal as self-protection—the same instinct Bram knows too well.

chapters.title: Dez's Father Knew Wren
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Dez's dad, the custodian, quietly reveals he found Wren's final letter years ago and never opened it, afraid of what the school would do to his job—or his kid. He gives it to Dez. The beat is generational cowardice and the courage it takes to break it.

chapters.title: Wren's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Wren's letter names Hargrove as a fellow erased student who chose to burn his folder, and asks whoever reads it to 'sign for me, since I never could.' The beat is the weight of inheritance: the archive needs a keeper willing to be visible.

chapters.title: Reassembling Priya
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Dez and Bram show Priya that her binder is already half the archive's restoration plan, and that Hargrove's file proves erasure hurts the erasers too. Priya returns—not to hide behind history, but to finish it. The beat is reconciliation through shared purpose.

chapters.title: The Night Before Homecoming
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The trio restores Wren's folder, prints the heritage display, and prepares to reveal the archive publicly during homecoming—knowing Hargrove will try to stop them. Bram rehearses saying their full, real name out loud. The beat is trembling readiness.

chapters.title: Hargrove Locks the Basement
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. On homecoming morning, Hargrove seals the sub-basement and threatens expulsion, offering Bram a private deal: silence in exchange for a clean record and a normal graduation. The beat is the temptation of the careful life, one last time, at its most generous price.

chapters.title: The Display in the Gymnasium
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Climax. During the homecoming assembly, Bram takes the microphone, abandons the sanitized script, and reads Wren's letter and the catalog's first page aloud as the doors to the sub-basement are unlocked by Dez's father. Students begin finding their own names. The beat is the choice of visibility over safety, made in front of everyone.

chapters.title: What We Signed
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Fallout: the district investigates, Hargrove resigns after finally adding his own name back to the archive, and the school establishes a public remembrance wall. Bram, Priya, and Dez become the new caretakers—openly. The beat is the cost and relief of truth.

chapters.title: A Locker for the Homecoming
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. At graduation, Bram signs the archive's final page—Wren's blank last page—with their real name and leaves a note in locker 214 for the next careful kid. The beat is quiet, earned belonging: the labels are off, and the door is open.
